Hon. W. B. NANTEL (Minister of Inland Revenue) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 96, to amend the Weights and Measures Act.
He said: This proposed amendment to the Weights and Measures Act has reference to the metric system. Under the law, as it now stands, the use of the metric system of weights and measures is permissible. The object of the amendment is not to make the use of this system compulsory, but to provide for the substitution of the international metric standards in use throughout the world, for the local standards now authorized by the present law.
The legal standards of the metre and kilogram, deposited in the office of the Minister of Inland Revenue, consist of a bronze bar and cylinder. We propose to put in their stead a bar and cylinder of platinum-iridium certified by the International Bureau of Weights and Measures, after comparison with the original prototype deposited and kept at the International Bureau, Paris, France.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

If my memory serves me right, and I think it does, the office was first established in Great Britain in 1855, and in Canada in 1891. I	lay	down	the principlethat	the	same	rules	which apply
to Mr. Speaker ishould apply with equal force to the Deputy Speaker. I have not found, in any of the books 1 have consulted, any written authority upon this point except that Redlich, also in 1870 in the same volume, at page 171, has a very significant remark. After having stated that the deputy speakership was established in 1855, he goes on to say that later on, in 1902, an assistant Deputy Speaker was appointed, and he concludes his chapter with these words:
The appointment of a second deputy was not ordered till the 2nd of May, 1902, and was a part of the reform of the rules effected by the Balfour Cabinet. In the debate on the proposal, which took place on the 11th and 12tli of February, 1902, the necessity of the provision was recognized, the Chairman of Committees being already, in modern times, overburdened with business. It was, however, suggested from several quarters that the new presiding officer should receive a salary, so as to secure a material guarantee of the independence of the Chair. He does now receive payment for his services, though at first the Government did aot accede to the proposal.
When an assistant Deputy Speaker was appointed, or, to be more accurate, when the office of assistant was created in 1902, the necessity for such an appointment had become obvious from the fact that the business of the British House had become so overburdened that not only a deputy to Mr. Speaker, but an assistant to the deputy, was required. Then, when thg office was established-and it was established, so far as my information goes, unanimously-the suggestion was made from several quarters in the House that the assistant Deputy Speaker should, like the Deputy Speaker, receive a salary. The object was to secure a material guarantee of the independence of the Chair; that is to say, that the assistant deputy, like Mr. Speaker himself, and like the Deputy Speaker, should receive a salary so as to secure absolutely his independence. What do those words mean ? If they mean anything at all, they seem to mean that if the office of assistant Deputy Speaker carried with it a salary there was more guarantee of his independence in the Chair. If we are required to pay him a salary to secure a guarantee of his independence in the Chair, all the reasoning which applies to Mr. Speaker should apply also to the assistant Deputy Speaker; and therefore I conclude that the rule was recognized, and that this

was a further form of it, that the assistant Deputy, like the Speaker himself, should abstain from politics.
I	must again refer	to	the	fact thatin	my consultation	of	authorities	Ihave not found any discussion as to the	possible breaking	of	that	rule	byDeputy Speaker. I have	not	found	in
any of the books which I have consulted that at any moment the Chaiman of Committees departed from this rule and took part in any political discussion. Whether or not Mr. Speaker, or the Deputy Speaker or Chairman of Committees, is allowed to take part in any political discussion in Great Britain, I say again I have not been able to satisfy myself; but from the very fact that the books are silent upon this point, I conclude that the rule has been observed, and I believe I am correct in stating that, on the floor of the House itself, neither the Deputy the Deputy Speaker. I have not found in the assistant Chairman of Committees takes any part in the discussion. If I am wrong in this I would be glad to be corrected; but after what examination I have been able to give to the subject my conclusion is that the same rules Which apply to Mr. Speaker apply also to the Deputy Speaker and to the assistant .Chairman; and, quite apart from any precedents, discussing the question simply as a matter of reason, it seems to me that the conclusion is not only obvious but irresistible, that the Deputy Speaker should be bound by the same rules which bind Mr. Speaker; that, having to discharge practically the same duties he should be subject to the same regulations and the same exceptions. The Deputy Speaker presides over the Committee of the whole House, over the Committee of Supply and the Committee of Ways and Means, and I need not tell hon. members that three-quarters of the business coming before this House is discharged in one of these committees. The experience of Parliament has forced the conclusion that the Speaker of the House should not be allowed to take part in politics, and that the same rule should bind also the member of the House who has to discharge the important duty of Chairman of Committees of the Whole", of Ways and Means and of Supply-that is to say, the presiding officer in that portion of the time of the House in which the House is occupied in discharging the major part of all its duties. As an abstract principle, therefore, I submit to the House that the Deputy Speaker

is bound by the same rales that apply to Mr. Speaker.
Now, I come to the other question, and the more practical one under the present circumstances: what has been the rule of this Parliament in this respect? Up to the present time we have had no rule on this point, and if I bring the matter at all to the attention of the House it is because, in my estimation, it is important that we should know exactly whether this rule ought to be observed or not. The Deputy Speakership was established in this House in the year 1881 or thereabouts. Mr. Bergeron, when Deputy Speaker, took part in political contests in 1892, in 1893, and all the time he was Deputy Speaker up to 1896. This was notorious; everybody knew it; but his action never was challenged on the floor of the House, no exception was taken to it, and therefore no blame can be attached to him for it. In 1897, the first year of the late Administration, there was a local election in the province of Quebec, and Mr. Brodeur, who was then Deputy Speaker of this House, took part in that local election in his own riding, Rouville. His action was challenged on the floor of this House. The matter came up for discussion. I looked at the discussion again before entering the Chamber this afternoon. The discussion was rather angry, still not too much so, and, on the whole, I think the sense of the House was rather that the Deputy Speaker should not take part in elections. I may say that I discussed the matter with Mr. Brodeur himself, and that he said that	he had	taken partin	the	local	elections,	but would
not take part in any federal election. I believe that from that day up to last year the Deputy Speaker has never taken pait in any federal election. If there has been any deviation from this rule I do not remember its being called to the attention of the House. I speak subject to correction, because one's memory may in such matters be defective. If there has been any deviation from the principle I would like tc know of it. So far as I am concerned, I think it would be a safe rule to adopt that the Deputy Speaker, like Mr. Speaker, should be debarred from taking part in any political contest. Last year the member for Champ'ain (Mr. Blondin) took part in a political contest.

I appreciate very much the tone in which my right hon. friend has made the proposal which he has submitted for consideration, and I am sure the House will be obliged to him for the review that he has given of the practice of Parliaments both in Great Britain and in Canada with regard to the matters upon which he has spoken. It is perfectly obvious that the position of Speaker in Great Britain and the position of Speaker in Canada are not upon precisely the same footing for the reason which my right hon. fjiend has mentioned. I do not recall that my right hon. friend mentioned another aspect in which the two positions are different. In Great Britain it is not the custom to contest the election of the Speaker in his constituency. That arises out of the first consideration to which he has alluded. It being understood there that the Speaker will be continued in office although the party which selected him may not be returned to power, it has not been the practice in Great Britain to contest his election. In Great Britain, I think, there has been no such con-



test for a very great number of years except in the case of Sir William Court Gully. I happened to be in England in 1895, and I very well remember that there was a contest, and that after his election Sir William Court Gully alluded to the fact that a departure had been made from established custom in his instance, and he expressed keen regret that that had been done. There was also a rather fierce controversy in the press of Great Britain, especially in the Conservative press, as to whether or not the old custom ought to be observed in his case, but in view of the very satisfactory results which had obtained up to that time, notwithstanding isome strong expressions of opinion in the Conservative press, Sir William Court Gully was re-elected as Speaker and continued as Speaker, until he resigned the office. In these two respects, then, the status of the Speakership in this country is to be differentiated from that of Great Britain, namely that the practice does not obtain here of continuing the Speaker, even if the same party is returned to power, and that nere his election is contested. At the moment I do not recall any instance-I speak subject to correction-where the Speaker in this House has retained the office beyond the parliamentary term even though his 'own party is returned to power. As a result of that, the election of the gentleman who has been Speaker has, I think, been contested in the same way as any other election. Under those circumstances-this is not exactly relevant to the question but I mention it in passing-the Speaker in this country is placed in a somewhat peculiar position and possibly sometimes a position of disadvantage, because he is not expected to pay any attention to his own riding from the political party standpoint, and at the same time he knows he will be confronted with a contest in the ease of a general election.
My right hon. friend has referred to Red-lich. On page 135 of the 2nd volume from which he has quoted I find these very significant words:
The complete aloofness from politics imposed upon the Speaker received its full extension during the nineteenth century, when it came to he considered that he must keep himself free from all political action outside as well as inside the House, even in his own constituency. He is thus the only member of the House of Commons who is not allowed, either in speech or in writing, to advocate the interests of nis constituents. The position in which his constituency is placed is accurately described in England as one of practical disfranchisement.

The latest historian of the House gives a capital description of the situation in the following terms: The Speaker's constituents not only do not go to the poll; they cannot, according to present-day usages, call on their represent tnve to vote either for or against any measure which may he before Parliament. As the Speaker never meets his constituents to discuss politics, one of the chief means of present-day political education is lost to them. PolitiiiCal organization is suspended in a Speaker's constituency; for a present-day Speaker has no need of any local party organization to secure his return, even if the deemed it proper to contribute to party funds. The newspapers in the constituency have necessarily to refrain from criticism or comment on the parliamentary conduct of its representative: and in nearly all the essentials which go to make representation the constituency is unrepresented. In the constituency represented by the Speaker of to-day, political life is dormant; for ail its outward activities, as they concern both political education and local poll tical organization, are suspended.
But no constituency complains or frets under its temporary and peculiar political disabilities. It is honoured in the honour done by the House of Commons and the country to - its representative.
In this country the practice in that regard has not been followed because it has been felt-and I might give illustrations of that even in recent years-that the Speaker still does represent his constituency and is entitled to press upon the Government the claims of liis constituents and even to set forth to his constituency the advantages which they have been able to enjoy by reason of his being their representative in Parliament.
My right hon. friend, in the course of his speech, has not alluded to one aspect in which the position of the Deputy Speaker is distinguished from the position of the Speaker, both in Great Britain and in this country. It has been the practice for the Deputy Speaker to vote on all questions upon which he desires to vote, even if they are questions of direct party difference. That has been the practice of all Deputy Speakers under the late Administration within my experience, and it has also been the practice of the Deputy Speaker under the present Administration. As far as I know, the same rule prevails in Great Britain, although I have not absolutely verified that by anything that I have found in the authorities upon the subject. It seems to me that the Deputy Speaker in Great Britain, as here, is not hedged about by quite all the considerations which have governed the conduct of the Speaker in Great Britain, and I quite agree in the observation of my right hon. friend that the status of the Speaker in Great Britain

has become an accomplished fact, not through any formal, definite written rules, but through custom and tradition. The status of the Speaker in Great Britain has been established in that way, and exists in that way at the present time.
The same observation, I think, might be made with equal truth respecting the status which the Speakership has acquired in this country. My right hon. friend has alluded to the debate that took place in this House in 1897. The discussion, and the difference of opinion, arose, not upon the action of the Deputy Speaker in taking part in an election, but by reason of the fact that it was charged that for several weeks during the session, while enjoying the salary paid to him for the performance of a particular duty, he had been absent from his post here and had neglected the duty which he owed to the House. Several members who took part in the debate on the Conservative side of the House at that time, notably, I remember, Sir Charles Hibbert Tupper, and the hon. gentleman who at present occupies the Chair in this House, stated distinctly that they saw no reason why the Deputy Speaker, if the House was not in session, should not, if he so desired, take part in a political campaign in his own constituency or outside of his constituency.
My right hon. friend on that occasion alluded to the practice which 4 p.m. had prevailed in the past, and drew some distinction between the action of the Deputy Speaker in taking part in a federal election and in taking part in a provincial election. Perhaps I had better give his words exactly. After alluding to the status of the Speaker in the House and the traditions which enforced his abstinence from political activities while he occupied the high position of Speaker, he went on with these words:
But if that has been the rule applied to the Speaker, hon. gentlemen opposite know as well as I do that while they were in office no such rule was ever laid down for the guidance of the Deputy Speaker. While I have no desire to enter into a discussion of the manner in which the Deputy Speakers who formerly held that office have discharged their duties on the floor of this House, hon. gentlemen opposite know as well as I do that, outside of this House, the Deputy Speaker was as much a partisan as any of us.
Then, further on, my right hon. friend continued in this way:
If it be a crime for an hon. gentleman occupying that position to take part in an election, and if it is to be the rule that he should not do so, for my own part, I am. quite willing to apply that rule in the future, if that be the sense of the House.
However, no action was taken by the adoption of any formal rule, and, if my information is correct, the rule which had been pursued before that time by the Deputy Speakers under the Conservative Administration h*s been pursued since. I am not sure that I can give any instance in which Mr. McIntyre, who occupied the position of Deputy Speaker in the last Rarfiament, interfered in any election, and I speak with reserve >as to him, but I think it can be very clearly shown that Dr. Macdonald who, although a very strong partisan, discharged in a very commendable way the duties of Deputy Speaker of this House from 1900 to 1904, did not restrain his political activities in the same way. In fact, I have noticed extended references to his proposed activities in certain election campaigns which were going on in the province of Ontario while he occupied the post of Deputy Speaker. My hon. friend the member for Bonaventure (Mr, Marcil), while occupying the position of Deputy Speaker in 1908, I think it was, entered upon a political campaign in my own province.

I invite his particular attention to one passage which I have marked, and which I shall not place upon the pages of ' Hansard.' I think my right hon. friend will find, upon looking at that particular passage, that it bears fairly well the stamp of pretty 'Strong political attack. My attention was called to these utterances at the time, and it was suggested that I should make some reference to them when the Speakership came in question in 1909, because it was well known at that time, and it had been definitely announced in the Liberal press, that the hon. gentleman in question was to be nominated for the

Speakership. But I thought that under the custom which lias prevailed in this country it was not worth while, or at all events not desirable, that I should raise any question of that kind and, as far as I recollect, I did not make any allusion to it. So, I think that my right hon. friend will see that the practice has not been quite along the line of what he suggests now, even during his own administration.
I do not at all minimize the importance of having the Deputy Speaker of this House placed outside the pale of party politics, so far as that can reasonably be carried out; but there are certain considerations in that connection, which would seem to be a corollary of what my right hon. friend suggested, viz., that the Deputy Speaker should be considered equally immune from attack. If he is to be regarded as outside the pale of party politics, then in respect of political attack on one side or the other it would seem to me that a certain .amount of eonsideraition .should be given to the fact that he is not to open hits .mouth upon party questions or to take .part in .electoral contests. I merely make that observation in passing, leaving hon. members to make any application of my suggestions that may occur to them in view of what sometimes takes place in this House.
The best course it .seems to m.e is to surround the Deputy Speakership, so far as it can be surrounded, with the same tradition of custom and of us.age that is [DOT]applied to the Speakership in this country.
My right hon. friend has alluded to the status of the Speakership, in Great Britain *and in this country, but he will look in vain to the rules of the British House or tQ the rules of this House to find therein the foundation of the status of which he has spoken, and spoken, as I admit, quite appropriately. It does not seem to me, in view of the course of affairs during the past twenty or twenty-two years in which we have had the office of Deputy Speaker in this Parliament, that we have had any such difficulties or inconveniences in respect to the matters to which my right hon. friend has called attention,, as to necessitate our making formal rules in that regard. If we are to make formal rules and to embody them in a resolution of this House, why is there more necessity for doing it in respect to the Deputy Speaker than in respect to the Speaker? We have not attempted to do it in the case of the Speaker and nevertheless the

status of the Speaker is acknowledged in this House, and my fignt hon. friend himself has borne testimony to the fapt that the duties of the Speaker under all Administrations have been satisfactorily and worthily discharged by the men who have been selected for that important position. If we attempt to define the duties and responsibilities of the Deputy Speaker in these respects by the promulgation of formal rules, it seems to me that it would be desirable to inquire why these rules are more necessary in the one case than in the other. If such rules are promulgated they should be very carefully considered, indeed. For this reason, it does not occur to me at the moment, even in view of the incident of which my right hon. friend has spoken, that there is any occasion at the present time for the House to make a pronouncement upon this question by resolution. If it is thought proper, when next the rules of the House are under consideration, that we should embody in those rules some pronouncement defining the duties and responsibilities of the Deputy Speaker in this respect, or of the Speaker himself, I would be prepared to consider that proposal, although at the moment I would not be prepared to say that I would think it desirable. I invite the attention of my hon. friend to one sentence to Redlieh which most truly declares that the status of the Speaker to Great Britain is founded in tradition and custom. It would seem best to found the status, not only of the .Speaker but of the Deputy Speaker, on custom and tradition. Under these circumstances, after this discussion and the frank interchange of views on this subject-.and I am bound to say that in the abstract the views of my right hon. friend do not differ materially from my own except in the respect that I have mentioned-I shall be glad if he will not press his motion and if he will let the matter .stand until we have had an opportunity to consider it more fully in committee when the rules are being revised.

speechtext: Of course, I would gladly accede to the wish expressed-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: ST. LAWRENCE SHIP CHANNEL-BOILERS FOR TUGS.
speechtext: As this is practically a substantive motion, it is my duty to inform the House, if there are any other members who desire to speak on this subject, that they must do so before the member who has moved the resolution commences his reply.

subtopic: ST. LAWRENCE SHIP CHANNEL-BOILERS FOR TUGS.
speechtext: Of course, I would defer at once to the wish expressed by my right hon. friend-especially since he has left the door open for further consideration-not to press my motion at the present time. I will tell him, however, why, in my judgment we should have a standing order upon this point. My right hon. friend has asked me: If we have no standing order in regard to the Speaker, why should we have one in regard to the Deputy Speaker? My right hon. friend has very properly stated that there are no Tules to define the duties of the Speaker, and that they are all to be found in tradition and precedents; but if at the present time I think it advisable that we should have a standing order upon this point, my reason is the difference in the interpretation which has been given of the duties of the Deputy Speaker. The Speaker never takes the liberty of taking part in an electoral contest. The Deputy Speaker has thought it within his privilege and power to do so. If it be admitted that the same rule should apply to the one as to the other, the fact that there has been a 'difference of interpretation with regard to the duties of the Speaker and of the Deputy Speaker would be a reason why there should be a rule to determine precisely the duties of the Deputy Speaker. With regard to the manner in which these restrictions have been observed by Deputy Speakers, I am not aware that Dr. Macdonald ever took part in an electoral contest, except after dissolution. But I am not sure as to that. As to my hon. friend from Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil), I still persist that while, technically, he may have spoken before a dissolution, in effect Parliament was dissolved and the electoral contest was on. His speech in Nova Scotia was made on the 9th of September, when the compaign had really commenced-a very lively and vigorous campaign, as all will agree-and the House was dissolved on the 17th of that month. So he was no longer Deputy Speaker, except in a technical sense.

speechtext: A certain leavening has gome on very rapidly in this matter even in Canada. When Joseph Howe, James W. Johnson, Sir Charles Tupper and Sir William Young were fighting their political battles in Nova Scotia forty-five or fifty years ago, it was the custom, unless I am very much mistaken, for the Speaker to descend from the Chair and make violent partisan speeches, and to be attacked like any other member and to answer like any other member. ['With all due respect to the hon. member for Ohambly Verchbres, it has been decided that the salaries of those who are not appointed by commission are subject to seizure.
It seems to me to be the general opinion on both sides of the House that it is absolutely urgent the Government should do something for those men whose salaries are inadequate.

This item covers the salaries of all excise employees, including the different classes of inspectors and collectors. There is an increase of $13,471.75. There are some new appointments and increases , of salaries. The salary of the exciseman is generally low; third-class excisemen start at $600. I consider that these salaries should be increased, and the increase over last year is to be applied to increasing the salaries of the lower grade officers in the department. The increase of an employee's salary is based upon a certificate from his chief that he is entitled to the increase.

Are these men in the
inside or the outside service?
Outside only.

When the
Civil Service Act was last revised, the gen-' tlemen who now sit on the Treasury Benches expressed the view, and put it. very strongly, that the principle of competitive examination should apply not oniy to the inside service, but to the outside service also. If there are any officers to whom the competitive examination should be applied, it seems to me that they are those in the excise service. Special qualifications are required of them, and I would ask my hon. friend if it is his intention to apply to that service the competitive examination system.

The question has not
been decided yet. I .suppose that if the outside service is considered as being on the same footing as the inside service, the same competitive examination may 'be required.

The duties of the various officials in the outside service differ very widely. For instance, I would not ask that the postmasters in the rural districts should be appointed under a system of competitive examination, and the same may he said of lightkeepers and officers of-a similar character. But in the Customs and Excise Departments it seems to me that there is ample reason why such a system should be introduced in respect of the outside service.

We already have what
may be called a competitive examination as to promotion.

If the competitive examination system applies to promotion, can any reason be given why it

should not be applied also to first appointments?

The first appointment is
generally made this way. The officer is appointed temporarily, and has to pass a Civil Service examination before he is permanently . appointed.
How long does his temporary appointment last?

We generally give the
employees time to pass the Civil Service examination.
How many distilleries are there in Canada and where are they situated ?
There are fourteen.
Has the distillery at Beau-port closed or is it still in existence ?
It was closed.
When ?
Last fall.

How long did the excise officer in the employ of the Government remain at Quebec or at Beauport, doing nothing and still drawing a salary from the Government, before he was transferred? I refer to David Murray, now at Prescott.
I am informed he spent one month at Beauport after the closing of the distillery, and was then transferred to Prescott.
Is the minister sure that that information is correct ?
I am informed that he was there about a month after the closing of the distillery.
I wish the minister would procure for us the exact date of the closing of the distillery and of the transfer of Mr. Murray to Prescott, and also tell us the duties now performed by Mr. Murray.

He is there as a first-class excise man belonging to the division at Prescott. His name appears in the report as being still at Quebec, but, of course, in the next report he will appear in the Prescott division. He receives a salary of $1,500 a year.

I quite agree that the salary paid to Mr. Murray is very reasonable, because I know him personally and he is certainly a competent officer. The information I wanted is as to the duties of this man at Prescott, whom he replaced,
and the factory in which he is employed as excise officer.
I am not in a position to give this information immediately.
How many breweries are there in Canada and where are they situated ?
I shall procure that information.

Would the minister also let us have the number of tobacco, cigar and vinegar factories in Canada ? Will the minister complete his statement as to the exact number of employees whose salaries he intends to increase under this vote ?
There is an item of $10,975 covering the statutory increases in salaries and a certain number of appointments. I have the names here of those who will receive increases in salary.

It is not the names of the employees I was asking for. I would like to know how many employees in the whole service are going to receive an increase in salary under this new law. If the hon. minister places a certain amount in his Estimates for salary increases he must certainly be in a position to give this committee the number of men wnose salary he intends to increase.
About sixty.
Do I understand that there are only sixty in the whole Inland Revenue service who are going to receive an increase?
I am speaking of the thirdclass excisemen.
How many are to receive increases in the other classes?
They receive the statutory increase.

Perhaps to-night, when
his Estimates are before the House, the minister could give us the total number of employees in the whole department who are going to benefit by this $10,000 increase. That is the information I desire. I can quite understand it may be a bit difficult for the hon. minister to give this information off-hand.
I can give the names of all the officers who will benefit by this amount.
That would take too long. I do not think the committee is interested in hearing the names.

Let us have the names.
Mr. BOIV1N: I bow to the will of the committee.
Shall I read them?
I did not ask for the names, but the hon. member for Pictou did.
I am perfectly willing to pass the book over to the hon. member for Pictou.
We want the names on ' Hansard.'
Do I understand the minister to say that last year on this appropriation there was an unexpended balance of $60,000?
About that- amount.
Do I understand further that the amount that the minister asks us to vote now, will not be all expended this year?
I do not think it will be.
What is the basis for this appropriation?	,

Perhaps it is a false
principle, but it is the principle that has always been followed by the department. We have a margin. We prefer to have more rather than less, but we do not feel compelled to spend the whole amount. If I cannot use that money to increase the salaries, it will return to the treasury.

I understand that, but
what I want to know is upon what basis the minister arrives at these figures. I am surprised, and not a little surprised, when the m.nister makes the statement that he is starting on a false principle.
I did not say it was a false principle. I said it might be a false principle but that it was the principle that had been followed by the department.

The principle is being
criticised very much and ought to be improved on.
I did not know it had been criticised.

That is hardly a satisfactory answer for us on this side of the House. We would like to know whether it is a false principle or not, and we might have some discussion on the principle before going any further. The minister says

that last year he had an unexpended balance of $60,000. We find in the Estimates a column for revotes, and the money unexpended goes under the heading of revotes. Looking up this particular estimate I see that in 1913-14 the amount was $551,807, and in 1914-15 $565,278. Here is an increase of $13,471 over last year, and yet the minister states that last year he had an unexpended balance of about $60,000. I want to know upon what principle this appropriation is based?

I am not ready to discuss, just at present, as to whether the principle is good or bad; but I may tell the honourable member that the department follows the method which has been adopted for more than ten years.
Now, we always have a balance of estimates representing a pretty fair amount. We prefer to have a little more than a little less, in order not to ask for supplementary estimates.
I am not opposed to that, because we have followed about the same principle.

It is because I think that this additional estimate will put me in a position to increase the salary of several of those employees whom I consider as being underpaid. The principle may be a bad one, but it was my intention to make those increases out of that sum of $13,471 which has been put in the estimates, if Parliament is ready to vote it. And should we adopt the Bill which may perhaps be introduced during the present session, I shall take this opportunity to increase the salary of those employees, because there are some of them who get but $800 or $1,000 though they have been in the service for quite a few years.

I have no blame to cast on the minister, those disposition are splendid; but I wonder on what basis he is distributing that sum? Does he take as a basis the number of employees, or the time during which they have served, or his own fancy? There should be a basis of some kind.
The hon. minister has said that there were fifteen or twenty employees who did not. get the salary to which they were entitled.
I shall point out to him that I am not asking such questions in order to embarrass him, but merely to get some information.
Shall those increase be granted by virtue of the new civil service law which has been announced in the Speech from the Throne,

and is the honourable minister in a position to tell us when this Bill shall be introduced? In fine, I wish to know whether the increase in the business of this year is taken as a basis for the estimate which we are voting.
I wish to know whether new offices have been opened for the collection of excise duties.

I say again that the same basis was followed this year. There has always been an additional amount laid aside in order to face those needs which the honourable member has alluded to. In fact the number of employees is a little larger than that of last year. We have 10 inspectors, 10 collectors, 28 collectors belonging to class A, 70 collectors belonging to class B, and 29 belonging to a special class, and then, 75 belonging to the third class. The number of employees is about the same, but we are obliged to appoint other men in certain localities when we open new collection offices. That is the reason of this increase and we take as a basis the experience of the preceding years.
If I understood the honourable minister aright, he told us that a temporary employee could not be appointed as permanent unless he had passed the Civil Service examination.

Exactly. When the candidates have taken the examination and a certain number of them have been successful, the permanent employees are selected among those who have been successful, and that without regard to. their political preference.

If the candidates are not all successful and the number of those who have passed is less that the number of employees needed, do you allow the unsuccessful to try again? Does the department take into account the political ideas of those who have passed their examination with success?

First of all, one must not mistake the exterior service for the interior service. As far as the interior service is concerned, we get our employees from the Civil Service Commission; but as to excise, the inspectors are appointed according to the principle of promotion, except in certain cases. For the higher positions we take but the employees who are already in the service. With regard to thrd class officials we take political recommendation into account, to some extent, the choice is made just about the same way as formerly.

Is the honourable minister
of opinion that the Conservatives are any better than the Liberals in this respect?
We do not care about that, and nominations have been made to the great discontent of our political friends.

I would like to know from the honourable minister if, when an officer gets into the department as permanent after going through a test for some _ time as a temporary employee and he takes his retreat, his years of service as a temporary employee shall be added to his years of service as permanent, in order to determine the amount of his pension? For instance, in the case of an employee having been in the permanent service for thirty years and in the temporary service for five years, shall those five years be taken into account when he takes his retreat?
When he takes his retreat his years of service shall count but from the date of his permanent appointment.

Must I understand that the inspectors of revenue who have passed an examination are the only ones entitled to the benefit of the salary increase paid out of those $13,471.75, because it is said in the wording of the item under discussion.
Salaries of excise officials and inspectors, &c., and salary increase according to result of excise examination.
Are those the only ones who are to get the increase which the department will grant?
There is always, in the department, a certain number of employees who never passed any examination; those in class B, for instance, like the collector at St. John.
Shall he not get the benefit of this increase?
He cannot get it directly; but the collectors in class B are apart and they get an increase notwithstanding the rules which apply to all others?
On the item, 'Stamps for imported and Canadian tobacco,' I see an increase of $5,000. Has there been an increase in the importation of American tobacco into Canada?

This increase of $5,000 is to provide for an estimated increase in the selling of stamps. If the revenue increases in the same proportion this year, we *estimate that we shall need $5,000 more for stamps.

Mr. MoGOIG: Is it on account of an increase in the importation of American tobacco or on account of more tobacco being produced in Canada?	.

This applies to Canadian tobacco and imported tobacco.
Mr. MoGOIG: Is this increase caused by an increased production of tobacco in Canada or'by an increased importation of foreign tobacco?

There is no more increase in imported tobacco than in tobacco produced in Canada; the proportion is about the same. Last year we had about a similar increase, and this year we consider that we shall need this increase to fill the requirements for stamps on Canadian tobacco and imported tobacco.
Mr. MeOOilG: On account of the great amount of dissatisfaction existing in different parts of the Dominion, particularly in the counties of Essex and Kent, where indignation meetings are being held by the producers of Canadian leaf tobacco, and where other meetings are being held for purposes of organization to endeavour to dispose of the present crop, which they have not been able to do so satisfactorily as they could wish, and on account of the general feeling that the producers are not being treated by the manufacturers as they should be, 1 would like to ask the hon. minister, as there seems to be an increase in the importation of tobacco, if he would consider having an increased duty placed upon foreign tobacco coming into this country, so that the industry which has bees established in Canada would have further protection.

I will give my consideration to the question.
Mr. MeCOIG: That is hardly a fail answer in face of the facts. If the hon. minister has been keeping in touch with present events, he must hate seen the great amount of dissatisfaction existing in the country, as the leading press, both Conservative and Liberal, are having front page articles every day in connection with this important industry. Not only in the two counties in the south-western part oi Ontario, but in all parts of the Dominion, there seems to be a great amount of dissatisfaction. The minister is" asking for an increase in the item for stamps to label tobacco of $5,000 ovct $120,000 last year. He should have some excuse for this, and [Mr. Nantel.I
know where the tobacco is coming from. If it is all coming from the United States, and if the local industry is being demoralized on that account, it is a matter to which the minister should have given consideration before the present time.

We have nothing to do
but to furnish the stamps for labelling imported tobacco as well as Canadian tobacco. I am not aware that any complaint has ever reached the department in regard to the matter of which my hon. friend speaks. What we do is to furnish the stamps as demanded by producers or importers. We consider that we need $5,000 more to buy stamps so as to be in a position to furnish stamps as required.
Mr. MeCOIG: If the hon. minister were satisfied that injustice was being done to the producers of Canadian leaf throughout the Dominion and that a larger proportion of tobacco is being imported into Canada than in former years, would to consider the advisability of increasing the duty on the tobacco coming in?

Does the hon. gentleman consider that the injustice is due to the fact that they import too much tobacco?
Mr. MeCOIG:	I consider that the producer is not getting fair treitment.
* Mr. NANTEL: Protection?
Mr. MeCOIG: Yes. If they are importing more tobacco and the manufacturers are using foreign leaf more than was expected, and if it were proven to the minister that there was great dissatisfaction throughout the country and that public sentiment would support his action, would he give the matter some consideration

Certainly, if I received
complaint I would give the matter consideration and would submit it to Council, because it is a subject affecting the general policy of the Government rather than that of the department only.
Mr. MeCOIG: I can assure the minister that there is considerable dissatisfaction in the tobacco growing sections of the country. A number of meetings have been held in the county of Essex, and I see by the morning papers that another meeting is to be held in the town of Blenheim. It means a great deal to the farmers of Essex and Kent in particular; and if the minister will consider the matter as he has told us he will, provided it is forcibly drawn to his attention-as I have no doubt it will be after the

meetings to which I have referred-I know :it will give great satisfaction.

Is there a ring
amongst the buyers?
It has been said that the buyers i3eem to take each a particular section and not to come in competition with each other.

Will the minister please
tell us what the Government is doing to encourage the production of home-grown tobacco?	,

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think I must remind the committee that we are skipping a good many items. The item now before the Chair is the ' Salaries of Officers.' If it is desired to take the Estimates item by item-
I think we should go on item by item.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: If that be the wish of the committee, I will ask hon. members to confine themselves to the item under discussion.

I desire to ask the minister why Mr. J. B. St. Pierre has been dismissed. A return brought down to the House states that he was dismissed because * services not required.' Yet it appears he was replaced by Wilfrid Gauthier, at the same salary.

Mr. J. B. St. Pierre was
dismissed on the 1st of May, 1912, for political partisanship.

That is not what appears in the return. It says :
J. B. St. Pierre, temporary excise officer; services not required; given four days' notice ; replaced by Wilfrid Gauthier.
And, while St. Pierre, who was dismissed was thirty-seven years of age, Gauthier who succeeded him, was fifty-eight. And the new man receives the same salary as the man he displaces. Now, if J. B. St. Pierre's services were not required, why was the place filled?

Mr. Wm. Gauthier was
never appointed to replace St. Pierre.
I see by the return that lie was dimissed.
Yes, for political partisanship.

That is not what is
stated in the return. Can any reliance henceforth be put in official statements
brought down by the ministers? I read in the return which I have in my hand and which was brought down by the Government; Jean Baptiste St. Pierre, 37, temporary officer, drawing a salary of $600 per annum.-Why dismissed? Services not required.-Four days notice-By whom replaced?-William Gauthier, age 58, temporary officer, at $600 per annum.
If St. Pierre has been dismissed for political partisanship, why is it not stated in this return? How, after that, can any reliance be put in official returns brought down by ministers, if they are not as a rule in closer agreement with the facts than this one relative to St. Pierre?

Was St. Pierre a permanent
officer?

No. He is a Montreal man with whom I am very well acquainted. I wish to know why he has been replaced by another, as that tends to show that the position was a necessary one. Was he considered unable to fill the position, and why does not this return make any reference to political partizanship?

Of course, there is a mistake somewhere. However, I am satisfied that Mr. St. Pierre was dismissed on the ground of political partizanship. He was a temporary officer and was paid at the rate of $600 per annum.

Was there an enquiry
held?
No.

The dismissal of this
temporary employee, Mr. St. Pierre, of Montreal, though it interests the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Verville) particularly, because he knows the hon. gentleman does not interest me nor, perhaps, other members of this committee. But what does interest us is the fact of a return brought down in answer to an order of this House moved for by the hon. member for Russell (Mr. Murphy) gives us information which is flatly contradicted by the minister from his place in this House. That is the important feature of this dismissal. Are the members of the House supposed to rely upon the information contained in the returns which are laid upon the table by the Secretary of State, or are they to rely upon the word of the minister? This is not the first time such a contradiction has occurred since the present Government came into office.
There must be a mistake somewhere, either in my papers or in those of my hon. friend. I will endeavour to ascertain where the mistake lies.

The subject of dismissals
has been discussed in the House from time to time, and we on this side have been endeavouring to get some accurate information as to the number of dismissals that have taken place in the various departments. We have reason to suspect that information brought down from the departments and placed upon the table of the House is absolutely unreliable. For instance, in one department of the Government there have been 476 dismissals within twelve months. Looking over the return, I find that about 300 of them are put down as having resigned. Men receiving salaries ranging from $600 to $1,200 a year, their only source of income, are represented to us as having resigned because they did not desire any longer to hold their positions.
What department?

The Post Office. Such excuses or explanations will not be accepted by hon. gentlemen on this side of the House. This afternoon we have had another striking instance of the misinformation that is being imposed on members on this side of the House, and I think it is time that the country be made aware of the fact that on this question of dismissals the ministers or officials of the Government, in order to conceal the record that they have made in this matter, are deceiving the people with regard to the information that we on this side of the House are moving for.
Along the same lines, ia connection with dismissals, I would like to know why Mr. Deland, collector of inland revenue at St. Johns, was removed.
For political partisanship.

I know personally that Mr. Deland has never taken any part in politics.
I am satisfied that he was not removed on the grounds of political partisanship. The hon. minister wrote to Mr. Deland notifying him of his dismissal, and the reason given in that letter is that notary Deland had a partner who meddled with politics.
What is the name of that partner?

Mr. Brassard. I shall call on the minister to read the letter, for in the return which I have in my hands, it is stated that he was dismissed for political 
partisanship, which statement is at variance with the facts. After that, what reliance can we put in those returns laid on the Table of the House.

Mr. Deland, notary, practised in partnership with Mr. Brassard; they were in the same office practically, and Mr. Deland's office was at the same time the excise office, and it was in that office that the organization of the Liberal party had its headquarters. We considered that these two things were incompatible, and that is why we decided to remove Mr. Deland for reasons of political partisanship; if that is not a dismissal on political grounds, give it whatever designation you please. Mr. Brassard was a candidate at the last provincial election, and it is in that office that his campaign was organized. We appointed Mr. Archambault collector of excise.

I wish to answer some of the statements made by the minister. Mr. Brassard was a candidate at the last provincial bye election which took place quite recently. Mr. Del arid was removed in 1911. Mr. Brassard was never an organizer, was never anything else but a good Liberal, like, I may add, all other Liberals in the county of St. Johns.
Has he not paved the way for his candidature there?

I cannot say; but the excise office is altogether distinct from that jf notary Brassard. I shall ask the minister to read the letter addressed to Mr. Deland, so that we may judge whether he has been dismissed for reasons of political partisanship. I say that the letter is in direct contradiction with the return, for Mr. Deland never meddled with politics. But Mr. Deland being in partnership with a man who took interest in politics, it was resolved that Mr. Deland would be dismissed on grounds of political partisanship. That is what the minister calls political partisanship.

The old proverb whicli
says: Tell me with whom you associate, and I shall tell you what you are, is very apt in the present instance. The facts are as follows : Mr. Deland practised his profession in partnership with the future Liberal candidate, and the excise business was being transacted in their office. The matter was brought to my attention and I considered that both things could not properly be combined.

My hon. friend's argument might have some weight if Mr. Brassard

had, as early as 1911, been chosen as Liberal candidate for the 1913 elections.
In any case, the information given' me was correct.
I wonder what view will be taken of jny case, considering -that I have as my partner the Conservative leader in St. Johns.
My hon. friend may be sure that if it was within the power of the minister to remove him as member of this House, he would do so.
If his partner was collector of inland revenue, I do not know what I would do.
Has the minister requested Mr. Deland to change his office?
I do not remember that I have notified Mr. Deland to change -his office. He was dismissed in November, 1912, more than one year after the election of 1911.
When was he dismissed?

He was dismissed one
year after I assumed the administration of the department.
For what reason?

For the reason I have
stated.
What proof has the minister of the partisanship of Deland?
Mr. Deland admitted that he was in the same office with Mr. Brassard, and I considered it was not proper to have the Liberal1 organizer in the same office with the collector of the Government.

Surely this is no sufficient reason and is not to be accepted by the committee. Here is a gentleman who has been a public officer for fifteen years. He has given entire satisfaction to the public and to the Government; he is known ail over the district of-Montreal as a gentleman who has never taken any part, active or otherwise, in election's. Then this hon. gentleman gets hold of the office of Minister oi Inland Revenue. No doubt he carries on an investigation regarding this gentleman. He finds out one morning that Mr. Deland is in partnership with Mr. Brassard, a Liberal. He does not request this gentleman to conduct the Government's business away from his law office, but at once concludes that he is a partisan and dismisses him. For the same reason it might be assumed that-my hon. friend (Mr. Demers) would have
the assistance of his partner, a Conservative lawyer, in the organization of the elections in the Liberal interest. Every one knows that my hon. friend's partner is a Conservative, but is that a sufficient ground to conclude that my hon. friend receives the help of his partner in the organization of his great victories in St. John and Iberville?

He seems to get a lot of help from some quarter. -Mr. BELAND:	The only and the true
reason is that some ardent partisan of the Minister of Inland Revenue wanted the position, begged for it, and said to the minister: This man is there in the same office as Mr. Brassard; Mr. Brassard, they say, is dreaming of being a candidate in the remote future; therefore dismiss your agent. Do you think public opinion will be satisfied with -such conduct? Public opinion will never be satisfied, and I think this will be another ground of reproach in the province of Quebec against my hon. friend when he comes before the electorate as candidate and as minister.
If that is the only thing to bother me, my conscience would be perfectly at ease in the next election.

I am sure the minister
h-as worse -sins than that on his conscience. What was the salary of Mr. Deland?
There was no Investigation held?
No investigation. Mr. Deland admitted the fact himself.
What fact did lie admit?

He admitted he was in
partnership with Mr. Brassard, and I had the other fact that Mr. Brassard was the chief organizer of the Liberal party in St.John and the coming candidate; and 1 considered, being told so by friends at St. Johns that it was incompatible to have the office for the collection of the revenue in the same office with Mr. Brassard, who was to be the next candidate in St. Johns.
-Mr. BELAND:	The only investigation
was a letter sent by the minister to Deland asking him whether it was true that he was in partnership with Brassard. The only question put to Deland was whether he was in partnership with Brassard and that was the only investigation held by the minister.
There was no investigation.

That was a kind of investigation. The minister sent a letter to Mr. Deland and asked him whether it was true that he was in partnership with Mr. Brassard. Did the minister send the letter? The minister is not in a position to say whether he asked-
I have not the record before me. I suppose that I wrote to Mr. Deland and he admitted in his letter that it was a known fact that he was in partnership with Mr. Brassard.
Surely the minister knew that beforehand.
I knew that and he admitted it.
You wanted the admission from Mr. Deland that he was in partnership with Mr. Brassard,
It was not necessary, he had made the admission.

What crime is it to have dismissed him?
Mr. BELAND I would like the minister to admit frankly that he dismissed Deland without a simulacrum of a reason. If he would admit that we would allow the item to go. Let him admit that he has dismissed this worthy officer without reason.

On the contrary, I contend that I dismissed that man for good reason and that it was not suitable to have the office for the collector of inland revenue in St. Johns in tne same office with the organizer of the Liberal party.
He was not then organizer of the Liberal party.
May I enquire from the hon. minister whether the Government pays rent in connection with the office of the collector of Inland Revenue at St. Johns?
There is a rental paid.

I understand from the discussion which has been started by the member for St. Johns that he is anxious to make some political capital in view of the next elections. I for one approve the decision rendered by the minister. The facts are as follows: Mr. Deland is collector of Inland Revenue at St. Johns, and practices in partnership with Mr. Brassard, the liberal political leader of the hon. member, the organizer of the Liberal party in St. Johns.
He is not my political leader.

At any rate, he is one of the leaders, and the organizer, of the Liberal party in the county of St. Johns; the hon. member, will not say the contrary.
Such are the facts which appear from that discussion, the leader of the Liberal party in the county of St. Johns practises in partnership with Mr. Deland, an officer of the Dominion Government. The rent for that office is paid for by the Government, and the hon. member tells us that this man was in office for a period of fifteen years. So he admits that he has been using an office, the rent of which is paid by the State, to earn his living as a notary in partnership with Mr. Brassard, the Liberal organizer in that county. The hon. member is horrified at the thought that Mr. Deland was Temoved from office. I think it will suffice to lay those facts before the public, and I have no doubt that the public will approve of the decision of the minister. Neither have I any doubt that the well-advised electors of St. Johns will approve of the minister's stand.

The hon. member for Dorchester has just drawn some conclusions on imaginary data. Mr. Deland may have got some rent from the department, but I know, having been apprised of it by Mr. Deland himself, that he has been paid only a very small amount as rental of the office used for excise purposes, and that he never was paid rent toy the department in respect to the office occupied by Mr. Brassard.
The hon. member for Dorchester, being unaware of the facts, has drawn false conclusions. He should have ascertained the truth of the facts before making such statements. The only rental paid by the Government was in connection with the office occupied by Mr. Deland, who was not practising his profession. Such are the facts, and I trust that public opinion will not be perturbed by the remarks of the hon. member for Dorchester.

I do not consider this the proper time to discuss the naval question, but I am prepared to discuss that question in my own constituency and I invite my hon. friend to come before my constituents at the next election. If I desire to coine back here I will be here just as surely as my hon. friend. As to the dismissal of
Deland, I regret that my hon. friend could not understand the discussion in French. I will repeat in English what I said. I dismissed Mr. Deland because he had as a partner the organizer of the Liberal party in St. Johns.
He says he was not.
He was the organizer. I was perfectly positive as to that fact and later events have proved it. He was preparing for an election and I considered that a good reason for dismissing him.

I am greatly amused at seeing hon. gentlemen opposite quite horrified because a few of their friends have been removed from office. They were not so particular in 1896, 1897 and 1898, when poor sectionmen on the Intercolonial were, without reason, being dismissed, on the ground that they were my cousins or my brothers-in-law.

You have appointed thirteen new men for the current year. You are asking for $13,000 for these thirteen new men, that gives an average of $1,000 for each one and there is nothing left for the others?

Now, the increase which I am asking for is payable to the sub-collectors of class B. There is an increase of $13,250 That represents the increase granted to those officers in the course of the year.

Is he bound to give all this time to the work?
M. NANTEL: Mr. Warren is a preventive officer.
Here is a very capable officer, and nevertheless, under the regulations of the department, there will be no increase forthcoming to him. Will he get an increase?

*No, for he is only employed as a temporary officer and is not entitled to an increase. Besides, there are applicants for those positions of $600 per annum in even larger numbers than we can appoint. Apparently they are satisfied with that salary.

Things are getting worse, if men are compelled by want to accept such a salary. Here is a most capable man-I am quoting Warren's case as an instance- even if it be a fact, as stated by the minister, that men of that class are available in unlimited numbers, that is no justification for paying starvation wages. Hunger will make people knock at every door, and be content with black bread when there is no white bread within their reach. I say that the Government has no.more right than any private citizen to take advantage of a man's straitened circumstances to make him work at a salary of $600 per annum, when-I take the minister at his own words-it is not possible to live nowadays on such wages. Such men are to be obtained in unlimited numbers, the minister states . . .

Is the hon. gentleman
aware when that man was appointed?

I do not know. Whether he was appointed last year or ten years ago does not make much difference to me. I know he is a first class officer, who is very capable and does his work conscientiously. There are a good many men in the various departments who could not pass an examination, and who nevertheless are competent. Now, without passing an examination, they cannot get an increase. It follows that the passing of examinations means a difference of three or four hundred dollars per annum.

mit increasing the remuneration of these temporary men.

Mr. Warren was appointed in 1891, and since that date, his salary has not varied, the rule being that all temporary officers must pass examinations before being entitled to the yearly increase of one hundred dollars. Mr. Warren was advised of the fact and did not deem it advisable to go up for the examinations. So we should not be blamed for leaving him at the same rate of salary. He was de-alt with in accordance with the regulations of the department.

I take this opportunity to state, following on the hon. gentleman from Maisonneuve, that such a rate of salary is inadequate, considering the increase in the cost of living, particularly in cities. We have just, now before us a striking instance. A civil servant was appointed in 1891 and has been in the service of the Government for twenty-two years, and his present salaiy is no more than $600 per annum.
Every week here in Ottawa, I have occasion to meet at my office government men who have been in the service for twenty or twenty five years. They are men who remained in the service under the former Administration at starvation wages. I am not aware that during those fifteen years, or rather during the eight years that the hon. gentleman from Maisonneuve sat in this House, he ever complained in this House that they were receiving too little. To-day the hon. gentleman is trying to turn this salary question into a party question.
Well the Government will go one better op the hon. gentleman's denunciations, for at this session, as announced in the Speech from the Thron-e, the Government is going to introduce a measure towards granting better terms to government employees, and we hope to have to that end the support of the hon. member from Maisonneuve. If the Government should do no such thing, then it will be time to complain.

When I enquired what salary, Mr. Warren was getting, it was for the purpose of finding out what was the remuneration of the men of his class. I was not especially concerned with Mr. Warren's case.
Several hon. gentlemen have stated that I have not done anything on behalf of the 
labouring classes. Hon. gentlemen are not in a position to know what is going on unless they follow assiduously the proceedings of the House. I let no opportunity go by without requesting an increase for those poorly paid men. To-day the increase of living in Montreal is 33 or 35 per cent as compared with 1891, and a rate of salary of $600 at that time was equivalent to $800 oi $900 at the present time. [DOT]

The increase from 1911 to 1914 amounts to 27 per cent. That is rather an important item.
The member for Dorchester charged me with trying to make political capital out of this salary question. I may answer that there is no need for my making any political capital in the constituency. I represent, through urging increases of salary; that does not further my chances. I have always been in favour of the increase of smaller salaries, whether in the case of workingmen or of Government employees, it does not matter, and I trust the hon. gentleman will take into consideration that very important question and find his way to changing the regulation which prevents granting increases to temporary employees earning only $600 per annum.

The hon. gentleman will admit that men, though they may have been in the service for a long period, are not entitled to the same remuneration as those who have gone to the trouble of passing their examinations.
Are they in a position to do so or not,
I cannot say. As for those who are unable to pass examinations, I am doing my utmost to be fair with them. I have increased the rate of pay for class B; I had the right to do so. I would be disposed to further the carrying of a measure granting a fair salary to every civil servant. Mr. Warren is responsible for his status; he knew what the regulations were, and he was dealt with as one not having complied with the requirements of the law.

As 1 understand it,
there is an increase in the item of salaries in the anticipation that a new law may be enacted to the effect that the salaries be increased. What is the lowest salary in the department at present?
In the excise?
Yes.
What increase does the minister expect to give on salaries of $600?

Will the regular increase be more than that on the higher salaries?
[DOT] You speak of the increase to be decided by the new law?
No. According to the item which we are now discussing.
Then those who are receiving $600 may expect to receive $700?
Next year, $700.

The minister has stated plainly and properly that men cannot live on those small salaries. Even $700 is rather small for one who has to support a wife and family. According to my calculations, from the number of employees which the hon. minister stated this afternoon, and from the amount of money wnich he is now asking for, the increase would be about $20 a year to each employee. Therefore, I presume that many employees will not get an increase. If possible, the increase should be given to those who need it most. Nobody in this House will say that $700 a year is sufficient for anybody to live on. I may be told that men working in other callings are receiving smaller wages, but that is not the point. We are supposed to be model employers, and it is a question of taking the money out of the people's pocket to give it back in some other way. Therefore we should increase the smaller salaries so as to enable those employees to meet their obligations. If the increase was double the amount, I would not be against it, because I am not against increasing salaries when absolutely necessary. During the discussion this afternoon, the minister stated that he had a surplus last year of about $60,000 over and above expenses. I am rather sur-nrised at the idea of a surplus in the department of $60,000 over and above expenses. I do not know whether we should congratulate the minister or not. Surely, if wisdom were exercised in forcasting the operations of the department, there would be no such surplus. However, if the minister is in a position to increase salaries, 881
I hope he will give increases to the small-salaried men.

That information is quite essential. Here we are discussing a vote for salaries of officers and inspectors which *shows an increase of $13,471.75.
