abolishing the examination.

I think the committee entirely agrees upon that question. Is the minister not in favour of so amending the law, having regard to the Civil Service Bill to be brought down by the Government in a few days, that an increase of salary could, in the discretion of the minister, be given to those poor men who have not passed the examination, and who are earning $600 a year?
That is a question which, no doubt, will be given due consideration when the Bill comes before the House.

I would be glad, and I am sure the committee would be glad, if the minister would promise to use his influence before the Privy Council to secure an increase of salary for these employees. I know his influence would have considerable weight, and I hope he will do all in

his power to obtain an amendment of the law which will enable such of these employees as are deserving to get a larger salary.

All the lower grade officers have my sincere sympathy. I have tried to increase the salaries of those who passed the examinations; as to the others, they will be given consideration. I consider, really, that if we could do something for them it would be advisable to do so.

A moment ago, in giving the list of breweries in the province of Quebec, the minister named the brewery or distillery, I think it is, at Beauport, Quebec, and he also said that this distillery is closed. Is the distillery permanently closed?
Yes.
Then why is it included in the list of existing distilleries?
We give it as closed.
Can the minister give us the cause of the closing?
No.
It was not closed owing to any order coming from the department?

No.
Mr. BOIViN: The department had nothing to do with the closing of the distillery?
Nothing at all.
Would the minister give the information I asked concerning Mr.Murray, and the date of the closing?
Mr. Murray was transferred from Quebec on the 1st of October, 1913, to Prescott. He took the place of Mr. W. H. Gerald, officer in charge of the Wiser Distillery, at a salary of $1,500.

I think that this salary of $1,500 is very reasonable for a man of the ability of Mr. Murray. I am not criticising his appointment at Prescott or his salary. Another item of information I asked from the minister this afternoon was why the distillery at Beauport was closed.
I am told that the distillery was finally closed in the middle of January last, and after Mr. Murray was transferred to Prescott, we sent another officer there from Joliette.

I am informed by people residing in that district that nothing has
been manufactured in that distillery for a period of almost two years.
But they were obliged to dispose of the stock on hand.
Was it necessary to keep an excise officer there for that?
Certainly.

A return which was moved for by the hon. member for Russell (Mr. Murphy), and which was laid upon the table of the House a few days ago, showing the number of employees in the Inland Revenue Department who were dismissed from the 10th of October, 1911, to the 12th of December, 1912, contains the names of a large number of these employees dismissed for political partisanship in spite of the declaration made by the minister this afternoon that political partisanship was not considered as a very great fault in his department. I am very much surprised to see that in some instances, not only in the case of officer St. Pierre, which was mentioned by the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Verville) this afternoon, but in the case of nine other officers in this list, which was 'aid upon the table of the House by a responsible Minister, in answer to a return moved for by a member of this House, there are nine names of persons dismissed, for what reason? Because their services were no longer required. They were not dismissed for partisanship, or because their services were not satisfactory, or because they had sent in their resignation, but because their services were no longer required. I can only take one meaning from that, and that is that there was no more work for them to do. The plain fact is that the nine men dismissed because their services were no longer required were immediately replaced by nine other men to do the same work. I would like an explanation from the minister as to how it is that these nine men were dismissed on six or eight days' notice because their services were no longer required, but were immediately replaced, by older men in many cases, with the same salaries, or in some instances, higher salaries, and why? Because their services were no longer required. It appears to me that the return is not a true return of the condition of affairs, that they may have been dismissed for political partisanship. It appears to me that if the Government dismissed these men for political partisanship, or for any other reason, they should have the courage to say in this return that they were dismissed

for such and such a reason, and not say that their services were no longer required, when they were immediately replaced by other men. I shall give the names of the nine men who were dismissed because their services were no longer required, and immediately replaced by other men. The first is John W. Bohan, temporary preventive officer, St. John, N.B., salary $300, services not required; six days' notice; replaced by E. J Clarke, 71 years of age, temporary preventive officer, St. John, N.B., salary $300. The second name on the list is Louis Basinet, 65, temporary preventive officer at Joliette, upon the enormous salary of $300 per annum. His services were no longer required. He was given a notice of nine days but replaced immediately by Dr. D. P. Lavalee, age 73, temporary preventive officer at Joliette, with a salary of $300 per year.

What	about the age
limit? [DOT]

These	gentlemen, 1
imagine, will have to go to Sunday school before they can pass this examination. The third man on the list is Dr. O. E. Milot, age 46, temporary excise officer, Three Rivers, $200 per year, services not required, twelve days' notice, replaced by Isidore Voisard, aged 61, temporary excise officer at Three Rivers, $200 per year. The fourth man on the list is J. B. St. Pierre, mentioned this afternoon. He was only 37 years old; he was temporary excise officer at Montreal at a salary of $600 a year, and his services were not required. He was given four days' notice and immediately replaced by Wilfrid Gauthier, 58 years of age at the same salary. The next man on the list is Mr. Richer, temporary assistant inspector of weights and measures at St. Hyacinthe, earning a salary of $600 a year; services not required. He was given notice of one month and eight days and was replaced by Mr. Champagne, age 33, at the same salary.
He does not qualify for that job; he is too young.

The hon. member for Shefford complains about dismissals. What would he have said if he had been here in 1896, 1897, 1898 and 1899. He complains about 98 dismissals effected in the department of Inland Revenue. I have here a list of 150 dismissals effected on the Intercolonial between Campbellton and Levis.
Mr. Chairman, I rise to a point of order. We are considering the estimates of the Department of Inland Revenue, and not those of the Department of Railways.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I understand that the hon. member for Rimouski is merely making a comparison.

There are complaints about civil servants having been dismissed on the grounds that their services were no longer required. I have in my hand a list of the dismissals made under the former Liberal Administration giving no reasons whatever. In that way were Desrosiers, Michaud and thirty-four others, whom I could name, dismissed without cause.
Do you not think, Mr. Chairman that the comparison is rather Overdrawn? I insist on the point of order which I just raised.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: As a matter of fact, the comparison is somewhat overdrawn, and if the hon. member insists, I shall have to declare the hon. member for Rimouski out of order.
I bow to your decision, Mr. Chairman. My object was merely to enlighten the hon. member for Shefford.

The hon. member for Shefford (Mr. Boivin) complained bitterly of the dismissals in my Department and he dealt with nine men who were dismissed for no other reason that that their services were no longer required. The return shows that St Pierre was dismissed because his services were no longer required; I could have dismissed him as a bitter partisan. He was president of the Club Choquette. He was a temporary officer but gave more attention to politics than to his duties. The total number of dismissals, is 83. We have in the service 500 or 600 officers and we have dismissed 83 since 1911.
No, you dismissed 98 in the first year.
I have the whole list of dismissals here amounting to 83.
That only shows that these returns cannot be depended upon.
Order, ordeT.

They were dismissed for
cause. Mr. Labelle of Joliette has been dismissed for cause.
What cause?
Defalcation.
Why did you not put that in the return?
Because he was a Liberal.

Why did you not
put that in the return?

All of these persons were temporary officers, and when they were appointed they knew perfectly well they could be dismissed without long notice. They have all been dismissed for cause, but m some cases, especially in St. Pierre's case, the reason was that their services were not required. I think I was justified in dismissing that man St. Pierre, and the same reason would apply to most of the other names -mentioned by the hon. member for Shefford.

I rose a few moments ago to draw the attention of the minister to the fact that while he tells us that there were only three men dismissed in his department, we have a return showing ninety-eight' dismissed and these were dismissed during the first year. There is another contradiction between the statement that the minister makes on the floor of the House and the return that was tabled by the same minister a few days previously.
I beg the hon. gentleman's pardon. This list is a list of all the dismissals up to December, 1912.
That is only for thirteen months. The date of the return is December 10. Can the minister tell us how many nave been dismissed since the 1st of December, 1912?

While the minister is waiting for the figures, I might mention that he stated a moment ago that the dismissal of Mr. St. Pierre was on account of political partisanship. If it had been stated in the return in that form I would not have brought up the case this afternoon. It seems to me unfair to dismiss a man for

tlie reason given by the hon. gentleman. There is no shame in anyone belonging to a political club. There are some hon. gentlemen who are presidents of clubs and nobody blames them for it. Therefore you should not find fault with anybody else. It has been stated in the return that St. Pierre had been discharged for political reasons, it would have been all right and I would not have said anything about it, but it is because it says in the return 'services not required ' that I bring the matter up. When he is replaced by another man it must be apparent to anybody who has any sense at all that there is something wrong. I would advise the minister to tell his department that when a return is asked for facts should be put in it as they really are because if that rule were followed we would not have all this discussion in the House.

The minister stated a
little while ago that in many of these cases he had been polite enough to tell these people that their services were not required but that as a matter of fact there were good reasons for their dismissal; in most cases it was because they were political partisans. I noticed that the first name on the list was that of John W. Bohan of St. John. John W. Bohan does not live at St. John; he lives in the county of Carleton which I have the honour to represent. I have known the gentleman all my lifetime.
I find the statement made that his services were not required. Certainly Mr. Bohan's services were dispensed with but Mr. Bohan's place was filled by a very estimable gentleman indeed, Mr. E. J. Clark who lives not a quarter of a mile from my own residence, a gentleman who is 71 years of age. I do not find much fault with that because there is not very much to do for an official of my hon. friend's department in that town. You will remember that we had a discussion about this work and the agreement was made with the late Minister of Inland Revenue that there would be no official appointed in that town. However, my hon. friend, from political exigencies, was compelled to make an appointment and he appointed a gentleman with whom I have no quarrel whatever and who, from a political standpoint, I think, was entitled to the position. Now will the minister say that the same reason applies to the case of Mr. Bohan as he has given regarding the case of Mr. St. Pierre? Had he any evidence to show that Mr. Bohan was a partisan?
I would like to know what record the min-
ister has of his conduct as an official and whether or not he was dismissed for cause or simply because they required a position for Mr. Clark.

Mr. Bohan was a temporary preventive officer receiving $300 a year, he was dismissed and, being a temporary officer, he could not expect to be kept indefinitely in the service. Mr. Bohan never protested against his dismissal. He accepted it.
What would the minister call a protest?
He never sent a letter of protest. I suppose he accepted the dismissal because he was-
What did you want him to say?
He seems to have accepted his fate very favourably because he was a kind of organizer.
Does the minister say he was an organizer?

I think I should give the same reason as for the dismissal of Mr. St. Pierre because the hon. member for Mai-sonneuve (Mr. Verville) does not deny that Mr. St. Pierre was an organizer or was chief of a Liberal club.

Does the minister say
that Mr. Bohan was an organizer and that that is the reason for his dismissal?
I say that Mr. Bohan has been dismissed for political partisanship.
Why did you not put that in the return?

The return states that
Mr. Bohan has been dismissed on the same ground that Mr. St. Pierre has been dismissed.

I want to give my hon. friend the minister a little more information. Mr. Bohan held another office under this Government and again political exigencies required that his head should come off. In the case of the other officer he was given an investigation and if my hon. friend will look at the evidence, which he will find in a return brought down to this House last year, he will see that the only evidence that was given against this man, Bohan, was that he was seen about a week before the election of 1908 going to the hotel in which I happened to be spending the night. On election day in 1911 he was seen

speaking to me on the street in the pres* once of probably three or four hundred people. That is the only evidence which they can find against Mr. Bohan.
Has he been dismissed?

Certainly. I want my hon. friend to remember that when the Conservatives want an office in the Maritime provinces they get it; it does not make any difference what it is. Sometimes they go through the form of an investigation; sometimes they do not, but the result is always the same. Oh, yes, Mr. Bohan was dismissed.

I suppose that I have
authority myself to dismiss him.

I think that kind of
evidence would suit my hon. friend.
It was sufficient.

I think that if he were seen speaking to the Liberal candidate, that would be quite sufficient, although surely in a free country like this, a man should be allowed to speak to whoever he chooses.
Mr. Bohan has a sister who was postmistress. She was dismissed, too, without any notice. My hon. friend the Postmaster General commences to look up now. He remembers that. He agreed to give her an investigation, but she has never got it yet. However, that will come up on another item.	.
It might be interesting to go down all the list of these nine men. We ought to have this return made complete. In the case of one man we are told that he was the partner of a man who, they were afraid, might be a political foe in the future. Another man was dismissed because he was seen speaking to the Liberal candidate on the street. I would like to know the . causes for the dismissals of the other seven men. The thanks of the committee are due to the hon. member for Shefford (Mr. Boivin) for bringing this matter up.
The total number of dismissals since I came into office is 84.

Slowly growing all the
time.
That is all. Many of these employees 'have been dismissed for cause..-
I thought you said 98.
No.
Why then is there such a discrepancy? The minister brings down a return to the House saying that he has dismissed 98 men. Now he says that he has only dismissed 84.
This is a second edition.
The total number of dismissals from 1911 to 1912 are 84.

Does the hon. minister
include in those 98 dismissals Mr. Des-marais, inspector of weights and measures for the district of St. Hyacinthe?
Yes.

On the list banded me this evening by the hon. member for Shefford (Mr. Boivin), Mr. Desmarais' name is inserted as having resigned. Would the minister be kind enough to inform me how he makes out that Mr. Desmarais has resigned?
Because he failed to perform certain duties. He was practically asked to resign because he refused to act,, and we put another man in his place.

I brought up this question of dismissal on March 21, 1912. The minister knows very well that Mr. Desmarais did not refuse to do his duty and he cannot produce any proof that Mr. Desmarais refused to do his duty. The Conservative candidate who was defeated in 1911 wanted to place one of his friends, Mr. Lemire, in this position and the deputy minister at that time wrote to Mr. Desmarais on January 18, 1912, as follows:
A. Desmarais, Esq.,
Temporary Assistant Inspector of Weights and Measures,
Bromptonville, Que.
Dear Sir,-I am directed by the hon. Minister of Inland Revenue to advise you that a charge has been brought against you of having, during the last federal election, acted as a political partisan.
You are therefore in consequence of this charge called upon to tender your resigantlon or show cause why your services should not be dispensed with.
I remain, sir,
Your obedient servant,
W. J. Gerald, Deputy Minister.
Mr. Desmarais wrote and said he had not interfered in elections, but he was forced to undergo an investigation. The minister told me that himself. They have a Conservative organizer in the eastern township who has been made commissioner to investigate all these charges. You can

imagine what kind of a trial a good Liberal would receive. The minister promised' me personally in this House that he would show me letters he had received making charges agains Mr. Desmarais. I went to the minister's office and he would not show them to me.

What reason did he
give?

He had one of his friends to place. This is what he gave in the House on March 21, 1912, in answer to my questions:
Mr. Ma ntel: A charge has been made against Mr. Desmarais by the Conservative candidate, Mr. D. Hayes, and acting upon that charge we gave Mr. Desmarais the notice that has been read. Since then Mr. Desmarais has left for Montreal and I have not heard of him since. We have been informed that he is working for a firm in Montreal and we have made no inquiry and decided on no dismissal.
Now, Mr. Desmarais had not left for Montreal ; but seeing that he had got this letter from the deputy minister and having a large family, he was trying to get another position because he knew what his fate would be if he had to pass through the hands of this particular organizer, Mr. Shurtliff who is employed the year round investigating charges made against Liberals. According to the return, Mr. Demarais resigned; yet my hon. friend the minister told us a few minutes ago that he had dismissed him.

In regard to Mr. Demarais, an investigation was to take place, but to prevent the investigation against him Mr. Desmarais went to Montreal and refused to perform his duties. We have dismissed him because he failed to perform his duties. No investigation was made, but if Mr. Desmarais had continued to perform his duties as inspector of weights and measures we would have caused an investigation to be made in his case.

Did I understand the minister to say that he had not made any dismissals in his department since 1912? I have a letter here of August 14, 1913, as follows:
Mr. F. H. Prefontaine,
Quebec.
Sir,-I beg to inform you that His Excellency the Administrator by an Order in Council, dated the 8th instant, has been pleased to dispense with your services as Assistant Inspector of Weights and Measures in the Weights and Measures district of Quebec, on the ground of political partisanship, to take effect from the 1st August, 1913.	[DOT]

This letter was written on the 14th ci August and the poor man not only did not have one day's notice, but was told he had to get out on the 1st of August, fourteen days before he received this letter. Naturally, Mr. Prefontaine was very much surprised when he received this letter. He wrote to the minister; explained his surprise; asked him what evidence he had and asked for an investigation. There was no answer to this first letter of his. He then wrote another letter and the minister answers, undeT date 22nd September, 1913:
I am in receipt of your letter with reference to your dismissal.
Mr, Huard, the defeated candidate in
Megantic, ^demanded your dismissal, on account of political partisanship. Having received several declarations corroborating charges, I considered I was obliged to take action. I therefore recommended that you be dismissed and council has sanctioned my recommendation.
Now, I should like to know what these declarations are.

It does not change the number, but an exact count has been made, and the number of dismissals in the department since I came into office is 84. Mr. Prefontaine was dismissed for cause- political partisanship-and no investigation was held.
A request for an investigation was made, was it not?
The case was sufficiently established and the hon. gentleman (Mr. Pacaud) himself will not deny that Mr. Prefontaine was a partisan.
I do deny it.
I received many affidavits from men upon whom I rely, proving that he v/as a partisan.
Did the minister receive a letter from Mr. Prefontaine denying the* charges and requesting an investigation?
Certainly. But I was in possession of the affidavits and considered the case established.
By whom were they signed?
By several persons.

But they might have been contradicted. We have had affidavits read in this House and contradicted by contra-affidavits, and they have been considered

sufficient to vote down charges against Mr. NANTEL: Well, let us call them ministers in this House.	solemn declarations.
I am sure these will not be contradicted.

I know Mr. Prefontaine personally very well, and I know that he has never taken part in politics since he was appointed to office. More than that, he is one of the most respected citizens in the county of Megantic. He is a Papal zouave, a Papal knight. He is a very old man, and has a large family, and by the action of the Minister he is thrown out in the street. I think that of all the dismissals made by the Government we must single this one out as most unjust and as one that would appeal to the consideration of any man. I must make an exception of the Minister of Inland Revenue (Mr. Nantel), because he is such a strong partisan that it would not appeal to him.

Here is a man by the name of Prefontaine who is dismissed by letter dated the 14th of August. He is told that his services have been dispensed with on the ground of political partisanship, to take effect on the 1st of August. Did he get his salary for the fourteen days' service he rendered from between the 1st of August and the date when this letter was written?
Yes, so I am informed by the accountant of the department.

This is a ve/y important matter. Here is an officer dismissed, who asks for an inquiry and is refused. We ask the minister why, and he says: We had affidavits. I think the committee has a right to know who signed those affidavits, what charges were laid, and before whom the affidavits were taken.
I would like it if the minister would give at the same time the letters he received applying for the position.
A return has been asked for; I believe it is in the hands of the Secretary of State. I have no objection to bringing down that return.
I would like to look over the affidavits.
I see no objection, they will be brought down.
I object to affidavits being read here, it is made a crime under the law.
In that case I have nothing to complain about.

I shall now read that of Mr. Jules Lapointe:
Canada,
Province of Quebec.
I, the undersigned, Jules Lapointe, of the parish of Ste. Julie, do solemnly declare:
1.	I am personally acquainted with Mr. Pr6-fontaine, of Lyster, in the county of Megantic, inspector of Weights and Measures.
2.	I overheard the said Prefontaine discuss
with much warmth and earnestness political questions, taking the Liberal view of them, on or about September 16, 1911.	.
And I do make this solemn declaration believing it to be conscientiously true and knowing that it has the same force and effect as if it was made under oath under the Evidence Act of Canada.
And I have signed: Jules Lapointe.
Received by me. .
d. McCullough,
Mayor of Inverness.
By whom was that declaration received?
Where was the mayor? Was he within the limits of his own town?
I cannot say.

If tha mayor was not within the limits of his territory, he had no right to sign as mayor. The mayor of a parish is an ex-officio justice of the peace only within the limits of his town. I oh-

tained a ruling on that point from the Court of Appeal.
The last affidavit which I read is dated Thetford Mines.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I wish to point out to hon. gentlemen that this incipient discussion over affidavits is out of order. The question could be dealt with, of course, before a court of justice. I understand it is an optional question and it is difficult to say who is right and who is wrong. I think hon. gentlemen should revert to the question.

Will you allow me, Mr. Chairman, to state along what lines this discussion is taking place? Our contention is that an officer has been dismissed improperly. The hon. minister assumes the responsibility of this dismissal, saying: I dismissed that man because I had affidavits justifying such a course. To that we reply: Had you granted an enquiry, we would have shown that the charges brought forward against the officer whom you dismissed were without any foundation.

The point of order which you have just decided, Mr. Chairman, was, perhaps well taken, but I think that we were perfectly justified-and I think the Chairman will uphold me in this-in asking the hon. minister to read to the committee the evidence upon which he based the dismissal of a government employee who had previously asked him for an investigation, and to whom an investigation was refused. The hon. minister read two documents which he first called affidavits, but which turned out to be solemn declarations. In these two solemn declarations the only evidence afforded is that the men who signed them heard the deposed employee, at some time or other, discuss politics. What the dismissed employee said, what arguments he put forward, in the interests of what candidate he expressed those arguments, was not stated. Are these the only affidavits the minister has, or are there other sworn declarations in connection with the same case?
There are more than those two.

I think this committee is entitled to hear the reading of the other affidavits upon which this man was thrown out of office.
Mr. Nantel: I shall now read a solemn declaration made by Mr. Edouard Roberge

and received by Mr. Thomas Legare, S.C. commissioner for the district of Arthabaska: Canada,
Province of Quebec,
County of Megantic.
X, the undersigned, Edouard Roberge, a merchant of the city of Sherbrooke, do solemnly declare:
X have for over twenty years been acquainted with Mr. I'rfifontaine, of Lyster, Megantic Co., the inspector of Weights and Measures. Ever since I have known hint, he has always been to my knowledge an ardent Liberal partisan, and I remember that in the early part of September, 1911, in the hall of an hotel in Thetford Mines, he discussed with me political questions in the presence of several persons, and that on that occasion he was defending the policy of the Liberal party.
And I make this declaration believing it conscientiously to be true, and knowing that it has the same force and the same effect as if it was made under oath, under the Evidence Act of Canada.
And I have signed,
Edouard Roberge.
Received by me, at Thetford Mines, this seventh day of February, 1913.

S. C. Commissioner for the
district of Arthabaska.
Those are the affidavits on which I dismissed Mr. Prefontaine.
Mr. BOIVIN [DOT] In accordance with the rules of the House, the hon. minister will, I expect, lay on the table the affidavits he has just read.
Certainly, they form part of a return which was to be brought down to-morrow in answer to an address.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I do not think the rule is the same when we are sitting in Committee of the Whole.

Was Mr. Prefontaine
given an opportunity of asserting whether or not this evidence was true or untrue? Were the declarations submitted to him''1
These are solemn declarations ex parte. I took the responsibility of dismissing this man because the evidence convinced me that I was justified in doing so.
Was the minister reading from the original affidavit, or from the return which has been brought down?
The return.
Now that the evidence is all in, perhaps we can proceed to make a little progress, and adjourn.

We have just begun with the evidence. Can the hon. Minister of Inland Revenue give the committee a state-

ment as to the success or failure that has been met with in connection with the experiments in the manufacture of peat?

That is not under my
department.

I wish to obtain some information from the minister in connection with some correspondence I have received with regard to wood alcohol and methylated spirits. I intend to ask him about certain officials, what they have done and what their particular work is. I think we should also have full information as to the amount of spirituous liquors manufactured in Canada, the amount collected from each distillery, and what it costs to collect these amounts. We should have the same information in regard to the breweries, including the total output of each brewery and the total consumption of beer in the Dominion of Canada. This information is particularly interesting in view of the fact
10 p.m. that a large gathering of persons in Ottawa this week are discussing these very questions, and that the hon. member for Dundas (Mr. Broder) has a motion on the order paper with regard to the sale of cigarettes. I would suggest to the hon. gentleman leading the House that, with the understanding that we could discuss later some of these matters, we might pass the first item for the hon. Minister of Inland Revenue.
Let us pass a few items.

It would he better to
take one.

I do not think my hon. friend will be able to obtain any information that will be of interest to him in so far as the congress that is assembled in Ottawa this week is concerned, but I am sure my hon. friend the minister of Inland Revenue will be only too pleased to bring down any information he may have with respect to the questions my hon. friend has asked.

I would suggest that the minister bring down also a correct return of the dismissals in his department. A return was brought down sometime ago and from the discussion this evening that return is evidently absolutely incorrect. Persons are set down in this report as having resigned or been dismissed because their services were no longer required whereas, as a matter of fact, they were dismissed on account of partisanship. I think the minister should be prepared with that corrected return the next time he applies for Supply.
All right.
I would like to know from the minister what Government employees have been dismissed in the county of Montcalm?
I do not see any.
And in the county of Joliette?
Henri Locas, of Joliette, excise officer.
He is from St. Lin.
Medard Forest, of l'Epi-phanie, M. Granger and J. H. Lafortune, of St. Jacques. These officers are of the Joliette division.
What crime had they committed?

Political partisanship.
Messrs. Louis L. Bazinet, C. Bourgeois, T. Rivet and L. P. Labelle, (dismissed for embezzlement), and lastly, Paul Ethier, of L'Assomption. I see no others.
Are there any left for dismissal? Can you tell me who has taken Mr. Bazinet's place?
He has been replaced by Mr. Lavallee, former legislative councillor.
How old is he?
I do not know. I found him quite capable of doing the work.
Is he related to a member of this House?
Not that I know of.

Who recommended
him?
I believe it was the member for that county. In any case, I personally am well acquainted with Mr. Lavallee.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I suggest that the hon. member address the Chair.
Well, Mr. Chairman, will you kindly request the minister to give me an answer and state who recommended Mr. Lavallee?
Offhand I cannot say; but he applied to me direct.
You said he had been recommended by the member representing that county.
I think the two answers are complementary.
I would like to have a detailed statement of the increases which it is proposed to grant out of the amount of $13,471.75.
The list of increases has already been given several times.
I may point out that among the men who are to. get an increase there is one by the name of Barette. Is he related to the member for Berthier (Mr. Barette) ?
No.
I also find that there is a Mr. Olivier. I would like to know whether he is related to the hon. member for Joliette.
Not at all; I am not even acquainted with him. Mr. Olivier lives at Berthier.
Address the Chairman.
There is no need of my addressing the Chairman; I know who are my relatives better than he does.

From the minister's answer, I see there is granted a more substantial increase to a gentleman by the name of Larue of Quebec, an increase of $300. Is he entitled to get more than the others who get $100 only?
Mr. Larue's salary is $1,400 only. He was appointed long ago, he is a very good man, and that increase is only fair.
He gets a larger increase than any of the others.
He is a Liberal.
There are so many kinds of Liberals, that it is a difficult matter to sort them out to-day.
That man got an increase because he took the management of the Quebec office.
That is not what I want to know. I am enquiring why he is getting more consideration than the others.
Because the amount is in proportion to what he earns. I must say I granted that increase despite some of my friends.

The hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Sevigny) stated a moment

ago that, until 1911, Mr. Verville had not asked for any increase of the workingmen's salaries, and the member for Dorchester stated that the Government was going to show its good will by deeds, actual facts. I may state to the hon. gentleman that what the workingmen want is more money, not facts. The hon. member for Maisonneuve made a very good answer, when he said that in 1911 salaries were fair; but that in the meantime have changed to such an extent that what was sufficient then, is now inadequate.
That is why I provided that amount in the estimates.

I am in favour of increasing the salaries of these poor people. I know what I am speaking about. I see them at work almost every day. They complain, and rightly so. The Government to my mind, should take the necessary steps to have the law amended so as to secure a fairer rate of remuneration to these poor civil servants. If the wish is that these men should lead an honourable life, they should be put in a position to at least make both ends meets. The only way to keep them right is to pay them a salary sufficient to enable them to properly maintain their families. It is not a question of party politics, but a question of justice. I do not blame the present Administration any more than the former.
Reference has been made to the removal of Mr. Bazinet, of Joliette, an ex-mayor of that city.
He was never mayor of Joliette.
It was his brother then?
Neither was his brother.

I know that man, he is an honest citizen. I am satisfied, in spite of reports circulated, that he has not interfered in politics. He had his own views, and every man is entitled to that. So long as you keep the names of civil servants on the electoral lists, they will retain the right to express their political views. If you are intent on depriving them of that right, strike their names off the lists of voters, and then you may rightly say that they have no business to talk politics. You make them judges of the conduct of the representatives of the people, and afterwards it is claimed that they have no right to open their mouths. That is neither fair no equitable.
I recognize that a public officer has no

right to speak on the hustings in election time, and still less to insult his opponents. Whoever does so is responsible for the consequences, and should his party be defeated, he is bound to fall as well.
Is the hon. gentleman aware that Mr. Louis Bazinet presided over political meetings?
I know nothing of the sort; I would like to have the proof.
Well, I am in a position to say so.

I know very well that the hon. gentleman would not knowingly deceive us. But I lay down in the abstract that no one should be dismissed before a thorough enquiry has been made, and not on a mere affidavit addressed to the minister, or on a solemn declaration, which deprives the accused of all chance of vindicating himself. O tempora, o mores! Is it not generally admitted that the greatest criminal has the right to be heard? I say that under British rule such a thing should not be tolerated. It is to be regretted that the spirit of partisanship should exact such reprisals. If the poor man had been given an opportunity to defend himself, the minister would not likely have taken the stand he did take.
Mr. Wilfrid McBeth, of Montreal a friend of mine of forty years' acquaintance, has been dismissed. I am in a position to state that he never interferred in politics, and if an opportunity had been given to him it would have been an easy matter for him to clear himself of the charges. Knowing as I do the kindly disposition of the Minister of Inland Revenue, I am .satisfied that some influence has been brought to bear upon him and that he has been deceived. When a political friend is anxious to get a job and is informed that there is none available, the minister says: I would only be too glad to help you, you have made sacrifices, try and find out something and we will give it to you. That man starts out and, under the spur of necessity, demands the dismissal of a political opponent.
Before resuming my seat, I shall request the hon. minister to seriously consider the smaller salaries, the starvation wages with which a large number of Government men, temporary employees who have been in the service for a period of fifteen or twenty years, have to be content. When a member is absent for reasons of health, and is unable to get his indemnity, right away some enactment is made and the member,
often a rich man, who could dispense with the money, gets his full pay. This House passes a Bill to assist a member of Parliament. Why should we not do the same to assist these ill-paid Government employees? The country is prosperous. I should even like to see the members' indemnity increased, and the ministers themselves increase their salaries, which would be only right.
If it is deemed necessary, on account of the high cost of living, to increase salaries everywhere in every department, let us not forget the small wage earner; wealthy men are able to look after themselves. People in ill-paid positions have no one to protect them, they are dependent on their daily earnings, they live from hand to mouth, and a mere casualty, a loss of employment through illness, for instance, may deprive them of their home; they are sued by the baker, the butcher, the grocer, and they do not enjoy such protection as is afforded to permanent officers, because they are mere temporary employees.
Their salary is not subject to seizure?

With all due respect to the hon. member for Ohambly Verchbres, it has been decided that the salaries of those who are not appointed by commission are subject to seizure.
It seems to me to be the general opinion on both sides of the House that it is absolutely urgent the Government should do something for those men whose salaries are inadequate.
Progress reported.
On motion of Mr. Pelletier, the House adjourned at 10.43 p.m.
Friday, March 6, 1914,
